rv.q: In London as in Manchester, this bizarre, inspired hybrid artwork strikes me as exactly the sort of thing the RSC should be doing alongside its more traditional core work.
The show is an inky black, nightmarish jumble of the play’s key scenes that wilfully trades off a certain degree of coherency but none of the intensity.
Her shiver-inducing rendition of Sail to the Moon is the show’s unarguable highlight, a moment of pure, piercing emotion that stands out among the frantic visuals and doomy music.
Whatever it is, though, it’s neat to look at and listen to but far too rushed to triumph.
It’s an electrifying night at the theatre which will live long in the memories of every audience member.
I can’t recommend it highly enough.

What does remain has been skilfully filleted by Jones and Hoggett - whose other collaborations (as designer and choreographer) include Harry Potter and the Cursed Child - to tell the story lucidly and with real dramatic momentum.
The result is bleak yet stylish, rushed but engaging, slick and yet a Hamlet-by-numbers with a nod to the age of vastly diminished attention spans and quick fixes.
Ultimately, Hamlet Hail to the Thief sacrifices philosophical depth for visceral sensory punch.
The cuts – the play is down from around three hours to an unbroken 100 minutes – strip out most of the poetry, and all the thought.
One of the most gripping, frenetic and visceral productions this reviewer has ever seen.

The Radiohead score sounds absolutely exquisite and invigorating, the Shakespeare is condensed but not dumbed down, and when combined with the endless invention of the talented creatives working on this piece, the combination is irresistible.
After an evening in which bodies have loved, fought and struggled desperately for control, the emptiness they leave behind is almost unbearable.
This is an exhilarating piece of theatre and proof that a risk can often pay off, especially when the source material, no matter how disparate, is placed in the right hands.
Hamlet Hail to the Thief barely lets you catch your breath, whilst looking and sounding incredible.
It’s an inspired fusion of genres.
Not a minute of the brief running time is wasted.
Endlessly moving, musically arresting and effortlessly personal, this production proves that sometimes the most contrasting things create the perfect match.
What we are presented with is a full sensory telling of Hamlet that would please the most ardent fans of both Shakespeare and Radiohead, respectively.
Bold, beautiful and exhilarating, it possesses an infectious energy that sweeps the audience along.
This is an innovative take on the text and a stunning production which will prove most effective to Radiohead fans.
The rock group’s gritty sound reenergises the rage and vengeance within the text, but the marriage between music and script isn’t strong as it could or should be.

Radiohead are a useful sauce to disguise something “good for the child,” the adaptation a decent gateway into Shakespeare, but no more than a chaotic experiment for those familiar with the Bard, alas.
A thundering whirlwind of a production that jolts us to the core.

Abridged and edited as a dance-infused play, this tragic tale is, in fact, a joyous chapter in the group’s oeuvre, bringing back the defining qualities of their previous successes: it’s edgy, grand, memorable, and somewhat visionary.

This dynamic, sometimes frenetic, sometimes oppressive but always gripping production brilliantly foregrounds all the key themes in Shakespeare's work, never sacrificing cohesion or complexity for the sake of brevity.
Far from being just a contemporary reinterpretation, this is a production that packs a punch, sending shivers through the audience with the force of its layered staging.

Instead, this collision between one of English literature’s greatest tragedies and one of the 21st century’s most politically charged albums, delivers a dark, electric and compelling theatrical experience unlike anything I’ve seen before.
The production demonstrates that even with significant cuts, the power of the story remains intact.
It’s a performance of angry confusion directed at anyone around him, whether they’re to blame or not, and it’s a fitting one to this particularly nightmarish take on the play...
However, while there were very many elements of this work we enjoyed, we didn't feel it came together as a particular coherent whole.
Though far from unenjoyable, Hamlet Hail to the Thief remains unclear about what kind of vengeance story it aims to tell, or what and how Radiohead can add onto that story.
I came away admiring the artistry more than feeling the tragedy.

cn.t: Critics largely embrace this bold Shakespeare-Radiohead fusion, praising its electrifying atmosphere and Thom Yorke's live score, though some find the heavily truncated text leaves emotional depth sacrificed for style.
